en: Shedding blood without fear of sin,
There was a cruel warrior too.
With agility beyond compare,
All the forty warriors,
From among the ninety one-humped camels,
Had eighty one-humped camels driven out.
They had them kneel at the treasury.
For all eighty one-humped camels,
They had pads and ropes prepared,
Had crimson cloth folded,
Red gold coins and yellow gold
Loaded on eighty one-humped camels,
Had gold piled in abundance,
And on all eighty one-humped camels
Had pile carpets spread,
Their humps standing proudly high.
To make them all match in appearance,
They fitted bridles of tin.
Of those who stood watching,
They powerfully drew the attention.
White cotton the size of a horse's head
They saw upon each camel's head.
Turning toward Bukhara,
Khan Manas's forty warriors
Raced one another in some places;
In some places the forty warriors
Wrestled to unseat each other.
When they halted, the forty warriors
Made a tremendous uproar.
Then, with one another,
They mocked and teased in a clamor,
Shooting wild sheep, chasing wild asses.
All the forty champions—
Their day for play had dawned.
The forty warriors went along the road.
Let us leave this here;
Ill-intentioned Khan Jakyp—
Let us begin the news of him.
Ajybay, of Argyn Khan,
Eloquent in speech, a master of words,
When the bright dawn broke,
When light fell upon the earth,
To rich Jakyp's court
Ajybay came and stood:
“My friend's father, oh Jakyp,
I come before you to speak.
These were words Bakay spoke;
Before rich Jakyp,
He told me to offer greetings.
Agree to what is said;
It is a debt upon your neck.
For your son, lion Manas,
Obtain a wife!
This Manas of yours
Is a leopard born bloodthirsty.
Hear these words, my saintly Jakyp.
This Manas of yours—
Your spring feeding a flowing river,
Your lamp found when you were near death.
You have no choice but to obtain a wife for him.
This is the request; agree to it:
Give a thousand dark camels;
Give a thousand black, blaze-faced mares!
Heed these words of mine, Jakyp;
Go as a prospective in-law, Jakyp;
Obtain a wife for Manas, Jakyp;
For such a son as Manas, Jakyp,
Let your livestock be a sacrifice for your son, Jakyp!”
Then Jakyp flared up,
Anger arising from the unseen:
“One who reared a harrier into a hunting hawk—
I shall not call Manas my son!
One who gathered madmen into a people,
Who reared a little falcon into a hunting hawk—
I shall not call Manas my offspring!
One who gathered wanderers into a people!
The harrier flies back to its place;
The madman returns to his kind.
The little falcon flies back to its place;
The wanderer returns to his kind!
He shamefully exposed my honor;
In Altay he scattered my livestock.
He drained my strength;
He diminished my herds.
My Altay was an excellent land;
The Black Kalmyks and Torguts
Were people with whom we shared respect.
I shall not agree to what you say.
For Manas, never mind a wife,
I shall not even obtain a bitch.
Since this Manas came to be,
Since he gained the name Manas,
He has scattered so much of my wealth.
This unbeliever distributed it.
To those who wandered from far away,
That Manas distributed
My horses among the forty warriors.
Into my court, where no one entered,
He brought a wandering rabble.
My vast herds, gained with hardship,
He made known to that slave Bakay.
Not heeding what he was told,
Not walking where he was driven,
That Manas you speak of
Became an outright brutal son.
He has drained my strength;
He has diminished my herds.
Manas has become utterly willful;
As I see it, God has struck him.
Pure gold and pure silver—
He has squandered it all.
When we migrated here from Altay,
I was left without livestock.
That calamity-bringing Manas—
I renounced him as my child.
I have offspring to care for me;
As I reckon, I have six sons.
I shall not agree to what you say.
Never mind a black, blaze-faced mare,
I shall not give my black yearling!”
Worthless Jakyp remained worthless.
All the forty heroes
He insulted as “his forty slaves.”
“Your fathers' graves, forty warriors!
You were dogs from forty places;
What men were you, if not dogs?
You utter coarse words;
Worthless Manas
You make into a saint!
Egging Manas on to needless deeds,
Your fathers' graves, forty warriors,
You plunge me into calamity!
I shall not agree to his demand.
My wrath is roused against Manas;
I shall not give a mangy young camel.
Turn back along the road;
To that reckless madman Manas,
‘He will not give a single yearling,’
Go and tell him quickly!”
When Jakyp said this,
Ajybay, of Argyn Khan,
Saw his life as no more than a hair.
Wishing to die, unable to die,
This was no enemy who pierced his lungs,
Nor could he simply kill him.
“Your father's grave, Khan Jakyp!
In the end you are a pauper.
Those vast herds you drive
Belong to your son Manas's good fortune;
If the time comes, they belong to winter famine.
Birches belong to the mighty mountain;
The many animals you cherish
Belong to the Black Chinese enemy.
Since your son Manas rose,
He made rib fat your food;
From the Kalmyks in Altay
He set you free.
A wretched people, scattered and worn down,
You settled in this Talas.
Because magnanimous Manas exists,
At all your tethering lines
You tied barren mares by the thousand.
Fire will engulf your home in the end.
You are a man bent on death;
Your six sons will bring about your ruin.
Oh, rich Jakyp, consider:
Can one who calls you father prosper?
Can a father be like you?
May the enemy spill your blood, barren old head!
May the enemy smash and destroy
The herds you begrudge, barren old head!
Were it not for magnanimous Manas,
I would make your blood flow;
Driving away and destroying them all,
I would wipe out your livestock!”
Lunging toward Jakyp,
Ajybay, born a lion,
His blood disturbed, his heart burning,
Allah's sun in the sky clouded over;
Sixty afflictions came upon his head at once.
“Of the magnanimous one we honor,
We must not strike the father,” he thought.
“One who sees his own child as an enemy—
Jakyp will never prosper in the end,” he thought.
“Such a thing does not happen even in Urum;
There can be no second Jakyp,” he thought.
Offended at Khan Jakyp,
The lion noble Ajybay,
Flaring up like a leopard, said:
“While the honored, bloodthirsty one is here,
Why should I raid his camp?
By striking Manas's father,
What inheritance would I gain?
With that ill-intentioned unbeliever,
Why should I lower myself to contend?
‘Your father will not heed you,’
I shall go and tell the magnanimous one!”
His sword ringing in its sheath,
Ajybay turned aside
And now went to Kartküröng.
Kartküröng, the peerless wondrous steed—
He ran up like a sheep and mounted.
To his dear companion Manas,
Khan Ajybay now set out.
Your lion Ajy traveled the road,
Covering much ground, sparing no horse,
Crossing rugged ridges and hills,
To the moon-pale yellow plain
That Ajybay arrived.
Into a tent sewn of blue cloth,
Big enough for forty warriors to fit freely,
For all the forty warriors
To play their battle game with knucklebones
And lie about with ample room,
Ajybay, of Argyn Khan,
Entered in a fluster.
Wearing a gray lynx-fur cap,
Taking a blue-mottled shield in hand,
Blue-maned Bakay boomed:
‘Oh, my child,
Azhybay of the Argyn khan,
Jakyp will not vanish from the borderlands.
While Jakyp's eyes remain open,
Manas's affairs will not prosper.
That fiercely wrathful brave one—
Though we might seize and slaughter him,
That ill-fated Jakyp
Bears the name of father.
“My father has become a fool,” one says,
But can one strike one's father?’
His mail coat flashing,
Royal Bakay boomed:
‘The span of days is six days;
Whipping my gray steed,
I shall travel to Bukhara.
To Temirkan of Bukhara
I shall try going as a marriage envoy.
Driving eighty red camels,
I shall braid the camels' tails.
“Give your cherished daughter,” I shall say,
Finding a way to ask.
If Temirkan heeds my words,
Eighty camel-loads of gold
I shall give without hesitation.
If Karakan agrees,
As kin by marriage, driving livestock,
Offering homage, feasting on fat,
Giving much attention to it,
Great treasure, countless gold coins—
Of a mighty khan like Temirkan,
Through his roof-ring let them pour.
Let us show boundless valor;
Bowing low before Temir,
Let us take Kanykey.
If he will not heed our words,
If he will not give Kanykey,
